« Ne votez pas, ce n’est pas votre gouve: “Don’t vote, it’s not your government” – Many Mohawks in Kahnawà:ke won’t take part in the federal election
À Montréal, pour échapper aux élections: In Montréal, to get away from the federal election, all you have to do is cross the Mercier Bridge.
Sha’tekarón:iase Cross (gauche) et Taiai: Sha’tekarón:iase Cross (left) and Taiaiake Alfred (right). Photo: Emelia Fournier
J’ai couvert des événements à Kahnawà:ke: I covered events in Kahnawà:ke when I worked on APTN National News, Canada’s Indigenous broadcaster. I knew that many Kanien’kehá:ka residents refuse to vote in federal elections. Many people outside Mohawk communities don’t know this, or if they are aware of the low voter turnout, they don’t know the reasons behind it. For the people of Kahnawà:ke, it is not a lack of interest in political issues or a matter of ignorance, but an affirmation of their identity as a nation. That is the view of several people in Kahnawà:ke. Other members of the community may see it differently, but most do not take part in federal elections.
‍<strong>À Montréal, pour échapper aux é: ‍In Montréal, to get away from the federal election, all you have to do is cross the Mercier Bridge. In Kahnawà:ke, a Kanien’kehá:ka (Mohawk) reserve along the St. Lawrence River, the absence of candidate signs and election events is immediately noticeable. Most residents will not vote in the April 28 Canadian election. ‍
Cela ne veut pas dire que personne ne s’: That doesn’t mean no one in Kahnawà:ke cares about politics. On the contrary, the community has two distinct forms of government: <l1>the band council, the Mohawk Council of Kahnawà:ke (MCK)</l1>, whose leaders are chosen by election, and <l2>the traditional Longhouse government</l2>, whose leaders are chosen by the Clan Mothers and community consensus. The Mohawk people are part of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, which includes six Nations: Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, Seneca and Tuscarora.
Taiaiake Alfred, spécialiste de la polit: Taiaiake Alfred, a specialist in Kanien’kehá:ka politics and history, leads the <l1>Kahnawà:ke Governance Project</l1> (Kgov). Through this initiative, community members gather to discuss restoring traditional government. On April 9, after a Kgov meeting, the twenty or so participants were invited to share their thoughts on voting in federal elections with La Converse.
« Personne dans cette salle ne vote », d: “No one in this room votes,” one woman says right off the bat, to knowing laughter. Winona Polson-Lahache, a longtime political adviser to the MCK, tells us she has advised Kahnawà:ke citizens against putting a ballot in the box: “Don’t vote, it’s not your government.”
De nombreux habitants de Kahnawà:ke resp: Many people in Kahnawà:ke abide by the <l1>Two-Row Wampum</l1>, says Elder Ka’nahsohon Kevin Deer. The Haudenosaunee treaty, still in force, stipulates that the First Nations and the Canadian government are meant to exist side by side in harmony, without interfering in each other’s affairs. Under this agreement, many members of these Nations refuse to vote.
<strong>Les conservateurs et les libérau: The Conservatives and the Liberals: “They’re the wings of the same bird”
« Les colons et les personnes qui ont im: “Settlers and people who have immigrated have their own government and their own way of doing things, so that’s their internal business. Just as we have our own government, and everything we do is our internal business,” says Ka’nahsohon Kevin Deer.
Les Haudenosaunee de Kahanwà:ke ne sont: The Haudenosaunee of Kahnawà:ke are not the only ones who refuse to vote in Canadian elections. During the 2021 election campaign, the <l1>traditional chiefs of the Six Nations of the Grand River</l1> forced an Elections Canada polling station off their territory. They felt its presence violated their treaty rights.
Ka’nahsohon estime que le fait d’attendr: Ka’nahsohon believes that expecting Onkwehón:we (a term meaning “first peoples”) to vote is an act of ongoing colonialism. “It all comes down to saying: ‘We are going to subjugate you, we are the power in place here, we are going to legislate over you, from the womb to the grave,’” says Ka’nahsohon.
Il affirme qu’aucun parti ne compte véri: He says no party really intends to tackle the climate crisis or respect Indigenous sovereignty by returning land to First Nations. “The way politics works, it’s about power, money and the economic engine, so animals and the land are often sacrificed because profits always win out over people. And that’s the problem... They’re the wings of the same bird, so to speak,” Ka’nahsohon laments.
Il ne prévoit pas voter. Il pense que ce: He doesn’t plan to vote. He thinks it wouldn’t change anything: “Because the province is still going to decide whether it wants to set up battery plants or whatever else,” he believes.

<strong>« Nous sommes citoyens canadiens: “We are Canadian citizens by force, through coercion”
Dans un éditorial de <em><l1>The Eastern: An editorial in The Eastern Door, Kahnawà:ke’s newspaper, reads: “In the spirit of the Two Row Wampum, the vast majority of community members boycott the federal vote.” For Taiaiake Alfred, it is less a boycott than a matter of not considering voting in Canadian elections to be his “civic responsibility.”
« Ma nation est la Nation mohawk, et nou: “My nation is the Mohawk Nation, and we have relations with another nation. So I have no hostility [toward those who aren’t part of my community]. It’s simply that my political community is not Canada,” Taiaiake explains. “We are Canadian citizens by force, through coercion. Not by choice. So it’s colonial for us to be considered Canadians,” he adds.
Taiaiake estime également que le vote de: Taiaiake also believes the Kanien’kehá:ka vote doesn’t make much of a difference. <l1>About 10,000 people live in Kahnawà:ke</l1>, which represents roughly <l2>9% of the total population of their riding, La Prairie-Atateken</l2>.
« Nous sommes tellement peu nombreux dan: “We are so few in a large riding that it doesn’t matter. So the only consequences are negative for us. It’s as if we were giving up our status as a nation, with no political gain,” Taiaiake sums up.
« Pour moi, la seule chose qui pourrait: “For me, the only thing that could possibly change the equation would be if a far-right candidate ran and there were enough of us for our voice to influence the vote. In that case, I could see reasons for us to vote strategically, as an act of resistance against that candidate. But we are far from that situation,” says Taiaiake.
<l1>Dans son éditorial du 28 mars, </l1>: In its March 28 editorial, The Eastern Door published the following: “There’s bad and worse, and then there are the Conservatives” – a reference to Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre, who has criticized compensation for residential school survivors and encouraged development of the Ring of Fire in Ontario. The newspaper also noted that the Trudeau administration made some minor advances on Indigenous rights, and committed some violations, such as the continued RCMP presence on Wet’suwet’en territory. But according to Taiaiake, neither Pierre Poilievre nor Mark Carney will truly advance the interests of the Mohawks.
« À mes yeux, il n’y a pas de différence: “In my view, there’s no meaningful difference [between the Liberals and the Conservatives] when it comes to Indigenous issues,” he observes. “Where has Indigenous participation in the electoral system brought tangible benefits? Here and there, maybe, but there hasn’t been any significant gain for Indigenous peoples. On the other hand, we have lost a lot of the notion of national independence in Canadian political discourse,” he concludes.
<strong>« C’est comme si ma voix n’était: “It’s as if my voice weren’t heard”
Sha’tekarón:iase Cross, un Mohawk de 24: Sha’tekarón:iase Cross, a 24-year-old Mohawk, speaks next. For him, voting in Canadian elections would be like voting for a prison warden. “My rights are constantly being violated. Whether my sentence is heavier or lighter doesn’t matter, it’s still a sentence. I have to get out of this prison. And to begin with, I shouldn’t be in this situation,” he says.
Le jeune homme préfère les prises de déc: The young man prefers community decision-making based on consensus, in keeping with traditional Kanien’kehá:ka governance. “I never really wanted to vote. I’ve always thought it was a bit of a strange process in our culture,” he explains. He has never voted in a band council election either.
« Dans la gouvernance traditionnelle, on: “In traditional governance, leadership roles are entrusted to people who are meant to hold them. It’s far from: ‘I like this guy because he conned a few people with his campaign promises and he’s a political leader, even though I didn’t vote for him.’ The so-called democratic model of elections doesn’t work for everyone. You can be elected without being the most competent person. In that case, it’s as if my voice weren’t heard,” he says.
<strong>« Quelle que soit la personne qu: “Whoever we choose, we’ll keep facing the same problems”
Steve Bonspiel, rédacteur en chef du <em: Steve Bonspiel, editor-in-chief of The Eastern Door, also refers to the Two Row Wampum: “We’re not supposed to meddle in their affairs, and they’re not supposed to meddle in ours,” he says.
« <l1>Certaines [communautés autochtones: “<l1>Some [Indigenous communities] vote</l1> and take part in federal elections,” Steve Bonspiel continues. “Voters want to choose their political leader. But in Mohawk communities, we know that whoever we choose, we’ll keep facing the same problems. Obviously, it would be easier to deal with a Liberal or NDP government than with a Conservative one. But it’s still the same beast, isn’t it?”
Le rédacteur en chef affirme qu’aucun pa: The editor-in-chief says no party is inclined to advance the Kanien’kehá:ka’s land claims. Originally, Kahnawà:ke’s territory stretched across roughly 30,000 acres. Today, the community controls only 13,000. With no promises to return ancestral lands to the Kanien’kehá:ka, Mohawks see no point in voting, Steve Bonspiel explains.
« Je pense que [le gouvernement] essaie: “I think [the government] is always trying to stall because it doesn’t want to give the land back. That way, they can keep building, keep developing on those territories. So there’s no space left, you know? That’s the biggest problem. If [returning the land] isn’t in a party’s platform, whichever party it is, it means they’re not really serious about relations with Indigenous peoples,” Steve Bonspiel concludes.
La Converse a demandé aux candidats de l: La Converse asked the candidates in the <l1>riding of La Prairie-Atateken</l1> what they plan to do to encourage Kahnawà:ke citizens to vote, and what they promise to do to serve the community if elected. Here are their answers.
Jacques Ramsay (Parti libéral) : « Je po: Jacques Ramsay (Liberal Party): “I will continue the dialogue with the Mohawk Nation of Kahnawake (Kanien’kehá:ka) in the riding of La Prairie-Atateken. My door will always be open.”
Dave Pouliot (Parti conservateur). Il in: Dave Pouliot (Conservative Party). He says he is holding consultations with members of the Kahnawà:ke community. “A Conservative government intends to work with First Nations in full respect of their rights and autonomy,” he says. He invites people to <l1>consult pages 32 to 35 of the Conservative Party’s Policy Declaration</l1> to read the statements concerning Indigenous peoples.
Alain Therrien (Bloc québécois, député s: Alain Therrien (Bloc Québécois, incumbent MP). He continues to go door to door to meet voters, but believes that responsibility for promoting voter participation lies with Elections Canada. “Mr. Therrien’s office continues to support everyone who comes in, as it has done for the past six years. This includes Kahnawake residents who have come to meet with him.”
Barbara Joannette (Parti vert) et Mathie: Barbara Joannette (Green Party) and Mathieu Boisvert (New Democratic Party) did not respond to La Converse’s request before the deadline.
